title: Gambler’s ruin in interviews
objectives: Apply ruin probabilities to interview questions.

screens.title: From £3 to £10
screens.prose: You hold £3 and bet £1 on fair coin flips. You stop at £10 or when you are broke. Press New paths to see other runs.

state.caption: Fair £1 bets from £3. Each path stops at £0 or £10.

screens.question: Fill in the chance of reaching £10 and the expected number of bets.

hints.text: A fair game keeps your expected bankroll at £3.
At the end you hold £10 with chance $P$, else £0: $10P = 3$.
$P = 0.3$. The duration is $k(N - k) = 3 \times 7 = 21$, from markov l10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: A fair game keeps the expected bankroll at £3. So $10P + 0(1 - P) = 3$.
byKey.r1c1: The fair-game duration is $k(N - k)$ with $k = 3$ and $N = 10$.

explain.text: Fair bets keep your average bankroll at £3, so $10P = 3$ and $P = 0.3$. The expected number of bets is $k(N - k) = 21$. About 3 paths in 10 reach the top.

screens.title: An edge of 60%
screens.prose: Now each bet wins with chance $p = 0.6$. Write $r = q/p = \tfrac23$. First-step analysis gives $P(\text{reach } N) = \dfrac{1 - r^k}{1 - r^N}$.

state.caption: Each bet now wins with chance 0.6.

screens.question: From £3, what is the chance of reaching £10? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $k = 3$, $N = 10$ and $r = \tfrac23$ into the formula.

byKey.fair: That is the fair answer. A 60% edge makes the top far likelier.
byKey.flip: That is the chance of going broke.
byKey.pk: You took $0.6^3$, as if you must win three bets in a row. You can lose some on the way.

explain.text: With $r = \tfrac23$, $r^3 \approx 0.296$ and $r^{10} \approx 0.017$. So the chance is $0.704/0.983 \approx 0.7161$. A 10-point edge turns 30% into 72%.

screens.title: Up by one
screens.prose: A fair walk starts at 0 with no floor. Will it ever reach $+1$? Put a floor at $-k$ first, so $N = k + 1$, and let $k$ grow.

state.caption: A fair walk from 0, stopped at +1 or at a floor. Here $k$ is the floor distance and $N = k + 1$.

screens.question: What happens as the floor moves away?

options.text: It reaches $+1$ for certain, but the expected time is infinite

options.why: That is the chance with a floor at $-1$. As the floor recedes, the chance climbs to 1.

options.text: It reaches $+1$ for certain, in about 3 steps on average
options.why: The expected steps equal the floor distance $k$, which grows without limit.

options.text: It may drift away for ever, so the chance is below 1
options.why: The chance is $\tfrac{k}{k + 1}$, which tends to 1.

hints.text: The chance is $\tfrac{k}{k + 1}$ and the time is $k$.
One tends to 1; the other grows without limit.

feedback.correct: Certain to arrive, yet with an infinite expected wait.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read both columns as the floor moves away.

explain.text: With the floor at $-k$ the chance is $\tfrac{k}{k + 1} \to 1$. The expected time is $k(N - k) = k$, which grows without limit. Rare long excursions make the mean infinite.

screens.title: Fair means even?
screens.prose: An interviewer asks: you have £5 and bet £1 on fair flips until you reach £20 or go broke. What is your chance of reaching £20?
screens.question: What do you answer?

options.why: That is the blurted answer. Fair bets keep the average bankroll at £5, so $20P = 5$.
You compared the two distances. The chance is your share of the whole range, 5 of 20.
That is the chance of going broke.

hints.text: What does a fair game keep constant?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the expected final bankroll.

byKey.b: You read fair as even odds of winning. Fair means the average bankroll stays at £5: $20P = 5$.

explain.text: A fair game leaves your expected bankroll at £5. At the end it is £20 with chance $P$, else £0. So $P = \tfrac5{20} = \tfrac14$.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose:
First-step analysis on the fortune gave every answer. From $k$, between 0 and $N$, with $r = q/p$:

$$p = \tfrac12: \quad P = \frac{k}{N}, \quad D = k(N - k)$$

$$p \ne \tfrac12: \quad P = \frac{1 - r^k}{1 - r^N}$$
screens.question: With $p = 0.4$, what is $r$?

options.why: That is $q$ alone. The ratio is $q/p$.

explain.text: $r = q/p = 1.5$. When $r > 1$ the formula still works: both top and bottom are negative.

screens.title: Check the duration
screens.prose: Interviewers like you to check a formula on the spot. Verify $D_k = k(N - k)$ for fair bets.
screens.question: Put the check in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: First step: $D_k = 1 + \tfrac12 D_{k-1} + \tfrac12 D_{k+1}$, with $D_0 = D_N = 0$.
Try $D_k = k(N - k)$: it is 0 at $k = 0$ and at $k = N$.
So the right side is $1 + k(N - k) - 1 = k(N - k)$, and from £3 of £10 that is 21.
Each bet moves you one step, so you need $N - k = 7$ bets.

hints.text: Write the first-step equation, then test the guess.
Check the ends before the middle.

feedback.correct: The guess fits the ends and the equation, so it is the duration.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the first-step equation.

byKey.d1: Seven bets is the shortest route, not the average. Losses on the way add many more.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the shortest route belongs.

explain.text: The first-step equations have one solution with $D_0 = D_N = 0$. The guess fits both ends and every equation, so it is that solution. From £3 of £10 the wait is 21 bets.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Write `ruin_prob(k, N, p)`, exact with `Fraction`, for any $p$. Then write `ruin_sim(k, N, p, trials, seed)`: play with `random.Random(seed)` and return the share of runs that reach $N$.
screens.question: Write both functions.

widget.starter:

from fractions import Fraction


def ruin_prob(k, N, p):
    """Chance of reaching N before 0 from k, betting 1 a time."""
    ...


def ruin_sim(k, N, p, trials, seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. Tests 1 to 6 need an exact `Fraction`, edges included. Tests 7 and 8 accept a simulated chance within three standard errors of the exact one over 20,000 trials. Test 9 runs one seed twice.

hints.text: Turn `p` into a `Fraction` first, and handle $p = \tfrac12$ apart.
For the simulation, loop `while 0 < x < N`.
`x += 1 if rng.random() < p else -1`, then count `x == N`.

feedback.correct: Exact and simulated chances agree within the noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: For $p = \tfrac12$ return `Fraction(k, N)`. The general formula divides by zero there.
byKey.test-7: The simulated chance is far from 0.7161. Check that each run starts at `k` and stops at both ends.

explain.text: The exact chance needs the fair case apart, since $r = 1$ makes the formula $0/0$. With seed 1 and 20,000 runs the simulation gives 0.7147. One run is a 0 or a 1, so the standard error is $\sqrt{0.72 \times 0.28 / 20000} \approx 0.003$.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Four puzzles at about 3 minutes each, 12 in all; keep your own time. The last, reported at hedge funds, is markov l8 (Which end do you hit?) in disguise. Four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the six answers.

rows: Fair, from £5, stop at £0 or £10. Chance of £10?
$p = 0.45$, from £2, stop at £0 or £4. Chance of £4?
A casino bet wins with $p = \tfrac{18}{38}$. From £10, chance of £20 before £0?
A drunk is 4 steps from a cliff and 6 from home, each step fair. Chance home first?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r4c1: Check the drunk: home is $N = 10$ and he starts at $k = 4$.

explain.text: The fair answers are $\tfrac{5}{10}$, $25$, $\tfrac4{10}$ and $24$. For $p = 0.45$, $1/(1 + r^2) = \tfrac{81}{202} \approx 0.4010$. The casino edge of $\tfrac1{19}$ cuts a fair 0.5 to about 0.2585.

screens.title: Follow-up: how long?
screens.prose:
You gave 0.7161 for £3 to £10 at $p = 0.6$. The interviewer asks how many bets it takes on average. For $p \ne q$, first-step analysis gives

$$D_k = \frac{k}{q - p} - \frac{N}{q - p} \cdot \frac{1 - r^k}{1 - r^N}.$$
screens.question: What is the expected number of bets? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: $\tfrac{N}{q - p} = -50$, and the fraction is the chance $0.7161$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $q - p = -0.2$ and the chance $0.7161$ into the formula.

byKey.fair: That is the fair answer. It is close, but the edge changes it.
byKey.drift: You divided the 7 steps up by the drift 0.2. That ignores the runs that go broke.
byKey.neg: Check the signs: both terms are negative, so the second subtracts a negative.

explain.text: $D_3 = -15 + 50 \times 0.71612 \approx 20.81$ bets, and a linear solve of the nine first-step equations agrees. It is close to the fair 21. The edge shortens winning runs but lengthens the losing ones it rescues.

screens.title: A trader’s edge
screens.prose: A trader wins each £1 bet with chance 0.52. She starts with £20 and stops at £40 or at £0.
screens.question: What is her chance of doubling before going bust? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: About $0.8321$: a 2-point edge over many bets is large.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $k = 20$, $N = 40$ and $r = \tfrac{12}{13}$ into the formula.

byKey.fair: That is the fair answer. A small edge compounds over many bets.
byKey.edge: You used the single-bet edge. The stake survives many bets, so the edge counts many times.

explain.text: With $r = \tfrac{12}{13}$, $r^{20} \approx 0.20$, so the chance is about $0.80/0.96 \approx 0.83$. A 52% edge on one bet becomes 83% over the run. It takes about 332 bets on average.

ideas: Fair bets keep the expected bankroll fixed, so $P(\text{reach } N) = k/N$ and the wait is $k(N - k)$.
With an edge, $r = q/p$ and $P = (1 - r^k)/(1 - r^N)$: a small edge compounds over many bets.
A fair walk reaches $+1$ for certain, but its expected time is infinite.

formula.name: Ruin
formula.tex: P(\text{reach } N \text{ from } k) = \dfrac{1 - r^k}{1 - r^N}, \quad r = \dfrac{q}{p}

summary.trap: Saying a fair game gives an even chance of reaching the target. Fair means the average bankroll is fixed: $k/N$.

quiz.prose: A gambler starts with £0 in a game that stops at £0 or £10.
quiz.question: What is the chance of reaching £10?

options.why: You started one step up. At £0 the game is already over.
At £0 the game ends before any bet, whatever $p$ is.

feedback.correct: Zero: the game ends at once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where does the game stop?

explain.text: $k = 0$ is the edge case: $\tfrac{1 - r^0}{1 - r^N} = 0$ and $\tfrac{0}{N} = 0$. At $k = N$ both give 1.

quiz.prose: Fair £1 bets from £7, stopping at £0 or £10.
quiz.question: What is the chance of reaching £10?

byKey.three: That is the chance of going broke.
byKey.half: A fair game is not an even chance. Use $k/N$.

explain.text: Fair bets keep the expected bankroll at £7, so $10P = 7$. It takes $7 \times 3 = 21$ bets on average, the same as from £3.

quiz.prose: Fair £1 bets from £2, stopping at £0 or £5.
quiz.question: What is the expected number of bets?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the two distances.

byKey.distance: That is the shortest way down. Wins on the way add more bets.
byKey.sum: You added the distances. The duration multiplies them.

explain.text: The duration is the product of the distances to the two ends, $2 \times 3 = 6$.
